strengths: Novel defense mechanism: operating at the KV-cache level to neutralize instruction-triggering neurons is a fresh angle that complements prompt-engineering and training-based defenses, and avoids modifying the prompt or adding extra LLM calls at response time.

The derivation connecting a DPO-style objective to a sample-efficient attribution loss (Theorem 1, Lemma 1) is a thoughtful attempt to ground the heuristic attribution score in preference optimization, and the motivating 'triggering effect' analysis (Figure 3) is an interesting empirical observation about how early response tokens flip clean vs. poisoned behavior.

Consistent empirical gains: CachePrune substantially reduces attack success rates across SQuAD, HotpotQA, and WildChat on two models (e.g., 27.86→7.44 ASR on LLama3-8B/SQuAD) while maintaining clean F1 and GPT-score, unlike Encode_Base64 which degrades quality.

Reasonable ablation coverage: pruning percentage p, masking strength α, number of trigger tokens k, layer-wise distribution of pruned neurons, and cross-attack (code↔text) transfer of the mask are all examined.
Relevant and timely problem; the defense is compatible with context caching, which is a practical deployment consideration.
weaknesses: The theoretical contributions are loose. The proof of Theorem 1 rests on questionable assumptions about the reference model (Eq. 19–20 appear inconsistent/typo-ridden, e.g., pref(yp|x) > pθ(yc|x) mixes poisoned and clean responses), the concavity argument for applying Jensen's inequality is not carefully justified, and Lemma 1 only establishes limit associations ('closely associated') rather than a real bound linking L^attr_full to L^u_DPO. The jump from Eq. 8 to the surrogate loss Eq. 9 is heuristic.

The efficiency claim is misleading. The paper advertises 'no extra test-time computation or LLM calls,' but attribution requires ~8 forward passes plus gradient computations per prompt, which is comparable to or more than the extra LLM call(s) used by test-time baselines that were excluded from comparison for 'fairness.' A careful compute accounting versus baselines is missing.

Ambiguity about how the mask is computed and applied: it is unclear whether attribution is per-prompt (costly, undermines the caching argument) or a single dataset-level mask estimated from 8 of 400 prompts (which raises generalization questions). Section 2.2 and Section 4.1 describe seemingly different protocols.

Security evaluation is non-adaptive and narrow: only the Abdelnabi et al. template injections are used for the main results, baseline ASRs on Mistral are already low, and there is no evaluation against attacks specifically designed to defeat cache/activation-level defenses, which is standard expectation for a security paper. The construction of y_p,* relies on strong assumptions (injected instruction answered first, hand-crafted 'Answer this at the end' prompts) that adaptive attacks could violate.
No comparison with training-based defenses (Struq, SecAlign, Jatmo) or detection-style methods (Abdelnabi et al.), limiting the ability to judge where this method sits in the defense landscape.

Writing and polish issues: numerous typos ('trigerring', 'greegy', 'interpret', 'undersdanding', 'On way', 'SQUaD'), broken cross-references ('(19) and (19)'), and leftover 'Note:' template text in the abstract and conclusion suggest the paper was not carefully proofread. No code release is mentioned, hurting reproducibility of the multi-step pipeline.
Only two 7-8B open models are tested; it is unknown whether the small subset of trigger neurons (0.5%) exists at larger scales or in models with different training recipes.

strengths: Novel defensive angle: pruning 'task-triggering' neurons from the KV cache is a lightweight, inference-time defense that requires no prompt modification, no extra LLM calls, and is compatible with context caching, distinguishing it from prompt-engineering and training-based defenses.

The 'triggering effect' analysis (Figure 3) is an interesting empirical observation: the first one or two generated tokens largely determine whether the model executes injected vs. user instructions, and the paper exploits this to make attribution cheap (N=8 samples).

Empirical results show meaningful ASR reductions (e.g., 27.86 -> 7.44 on SQuAD for Llama3-8B) while roughly maintaining clean F1, with ablations over pruning ratio p, masking strength alpha, trigger-token count k, and a preliminary transfer experiment across text/code attacks (Table 4).
The analysis of pruned-neuron distribution across layers (Figure 5) provides some mechanistic insight consistent with prior work on middle layers capturing abstract concepts.
weaknesses: The theoretical contribution is not sound as stated. Theorem 1 claims L^u_DPO is an 'upperbound' of the DPO objective, but the Jensen's inequality step yields a bound on E[log sigma(beta*S)], and the authors then simply drop sigma and log to define L^u_DPO = E[S], which is not a valid upper bound. Lemma 1 is only a statement about limits ('closely associated') and its proof is loose (e.g., unjustified limit exchanges in Eqs. 38-45); the proof also contains apparent typos (e.g., condition (20) should presumably read p_ref(y^p|x) > p_theta(y^p|x), and 'With (19) and (19)').

Methodological details needed for reproducibility are missing: how gradients in Eq. (3) are computed with respect to KV-cache entries (intermediate, non-leaf activations during autoregressive generation) is not explained; how exactly the paired clean/poisoned responses y_c*/y_p* are constructed at attribution time depends on attack-format assumptions; no code or reproducibility statement is provided.

Evaluation against strong or adaptive attacks is absent. The evaluation relies on the random injected instructions of Abdelnabi et al. (2024) plus manually inserted prompts; there is no adaptive-attacker analysis (e.g., an attacker who varies instruction phrasing to evade a fixed mask), no comparison to optimization-based attack families, and no comparison with training-based or test-time defenses beyond weak prompt-engineering baselines (Delimiting, Datamarking, Base64).

The construction of y_p* via the injected string 'Answer this at the end.' and the triggering analysis itself admit that the effect disappears when injected instructions are answered at the end, raising questions about robustness of the defense across attack formats; only a single narrow transfer experiment addresses this.

Limited scope: only two 7-8B models, three datasets, small evaluation pools (400 prompts, 8 attribution samples, 3 trials), and low absolute ASR baselines in some settings (e.g., Mistral Vanilla ASR of 9.01 on SQuAD), which makes some gains hard to interpret; generalization to larger models or agentic settings is untested.

The subset definition Phi in Eq. (13) is ad hoc: the condition a_p^norm > a_c^norm together with |a_p^norm - a_c^norm| > 2*min(|a_p^norm|, |a_c^norm|) is partly redundant, and constants (2, k=1, p=0.5, N=8) are not justified or sensitivity-analyzed.

Writing quality is well below the venue standard: numerous grammatical and typographical errors throughout ('On way', 'interprete', 'perference', 'greegy decoding', 'experiemnt', 'posioned', 'experiments differen values'), broken citation keys ('gem, 2025; ope, 2025'), ill-formed notation in Eq. (5) (tau defined via 'sup_tau tau in R Pr(...) <= p'), and odd 'Note:' addenda in the abstract and conclusion that do not belong in a research paper.

strengths: The core idea is novel and mechanistically interesting: defending against indirect prompt injection by attributing the data-vs-instruction behavioral difference to specific KV-cache neurons and pruning them, rather than modifying the prompt or adding test-time LLM calls. This is a fresh angle relative to prompt-engineering (delimiting/datamarking/spotlighting) and training-based defenses.
The method is lightweight in principle and plausibly compatible with context caching, where a cached context's KV cache needs to be pruned once and reused.

The paper includes a reasonable set of ablations: number of trigger tokens k, masking strength alpha, prune ratio p (Figure 4), layer/key-value distribution of pruned neurons (Figure 5), and transfer of masks between code-based and text-based attacks (Table 4).

The empirical results on two models (LLama3-8B, Mistral-7B) and three datasets (SQuAD, HotpotQA, WildChat) show substantial ASR reductions while maintaining F1/GPT-score, supporting the central claim within the evaluated scope.

The observed 'triggering effect' (Figure 3, Figure 7) — that one or two early tokens can flip the model between clean and poisoned behavior — is an interesting empirical finding in its own right and motivates the k-token attribution loss.
The problem (indirect prompt injection) is timely and clearly relevant to CL/NLP; the paper positions itself well against related defense work.
weaknesses: Strong and potentially unrealistic assumptions: the method requires (a) knowing the token indices cs, ce marking the user-specified context, and (b) constructing the poisoned response y_p by locating/concatenating the injected instruction (Section 2.3, Figure 6). In real deployments the injection span and content are unknown; the paper does not discuss how the pipeline would work when these must be inferred, which limits practical impact.

The 'no extra test-time computation' claim is overstated: feature attribution requires decoding candidate clean/poisoned responses (with and without prompt modifications) for N=8 samples per context. This is amortized only under context caching with repeated identical contexts; for fresh contexts it constitutes significant extra decoding cost.

The theoretical development is loose. Theorem 1's 'upper bound' derivation has apparent errors and sign ambiguities (e.g., Eq. (20) states pref(yp|x) > pθ(yc|x), which looks like a typo; the concavity argument and Jensen application are glossed over; the sign convention of the DPO objective relative to defending seems inconsistent). Lemma 1 only establishes limit associations (→ ±∞), which is weak support for using L^attr in Eq. (9); the final loss is essentially heuristic, and the paper should be more explicit about this.

Adversarial robustness is not assessed against adaptive attacks. The triggering effect is acknowledged to disappear 'when the injected instructions are answered in the end' (Figure 3 note), and attacks that spread triggers across tokens or are optimized against attribution would likely degrade the defense; no such evaluation is included.

Baseline coverage is narrow: only prompt-engineering defenses are compared; training-based defenses (Struq, Piet et al.), detection-based, and test-time workflow defenses (Wang et al., Jia et al.) are excluded by construction. CachePrune is claimed complementary to these, but no experiment demonstrates complementarity empirically.

Reproducibility concerns: no code release is mentioned; several design choices are under-specified or ad hoc (e.g., the '2 · min' condition defining Φ in Eq. (13), how N=8 samples are drawn, details of the WildChat 'attack' construction), and the small evaluation sets (400 prompts, 3 trials) plus greedy-decoding ASR leave uncertainty about variance and generality.

Writing quality needs improvement: numerous typos and grammatical issues ('interprete', 'perference', 'experiemnt', 'greegy', 'Waswani', 'correspondinglly'), and the odd 'Note:' sentences at the end of the Abstract and Discussion read as placeholders and should be removed or integrated properly.

Only 7–8B open models are evaluated; it is unclear whether the small subset of 'task-triggering neurons' (0.5%) exists with similar concentration in larger or API-only models, limiting claims of generality.

strengths: Novel and interesting defense direction: intervening directly on the KV cache via gradient-based (integrated-gradients-style) neuron attribution, which leaves prompts untouched and adds no test-time LLM calls, making it complementary to prompt-engineering and workflow-based defenses.

A thoughtful conceptual framing: connecting the defense signal to an upper bound of the DPO objective (Theorem 1, Lemma 1) and the observed 'triggering effect' (only 1-2 initial tokens determine clean vs. poisoned generation), which motivates a sample-efficient attribution loss (k=1, N=8 samples).

Reasonably comprehensive empirical validation: three LLMs (LLaMA3-8B, Mistral-7B, Phi-3.5-mini), three tasks (SQuAD, HotpotQA, WildChat summarization), multiple prompt-engineering baselines, and extensive ablations (pruning ratio p, k, alpha, N, subset Phi in Table 5).

Good security-minded evaluation practices for this venue: mask transferability across attack instructions (Figure 5) and across code/text injection types (Table 2), plus a GCG-based adaptive attack analysis (Appendix G).
Compatibility with prompt/context caching infrastructures is a practical advantage for deployment.
Reproducibility aids: metric computation code (Listings 1-3), judging prompts, adaptive-attack configuration, and dataset splits are described or provided.
weaknesses: Writing quality is below the bar: frequent typos and grammatical errors throughout (e.g., 'trigerring', 'perference', 'interprete', 'enforce', 'transferrable', 'discretion between data and instructions'), and confusing passages (e.g., the Encode_Base64 analysis sentence 'resulting in the model understanding the context' appears to be missing a negation; '(20) and (20)' in the proof).

Threat-model assumptions are significant and should temper the security claims: the defense requires (a) known context boundaries, (b) access to a pool of ~400 prompts with known attack instructions to elicit clean/poisoned response pairs for attribution, and (c) the assumption that poisoned responses begin with answering the injected instruction (used to construct y_p* via 'Answer this at the end.'). Generalization to truly unseen attacks is only partially addressed by the transferability experiments.

The adaptive attack design (Appendix G) is questionable: the attacker optimizes the authors' own preferential attribution loss (13) rather than directly maximizing attack success under the defense, and the claim that 'CachePrune is immune to such attack' on LLaMA3-8B is an overstatement based on a single, possibly ill-suited adaptive objective. A stronger adaptive evaluation would directly attack the ASR under the defense.

No comparison with training-based defenses (StruQ, SecAlign, Jatmo) or detection+filtering methods, even as reference points; the fairness argument (different compute regimes) is reasonable but the paper would benefit from at least discussing expected trade-offs quantitatively.

Some empirical gaps: response-quality F1 values are low in absolute terms for the free-form setup (acknowledged in Appendix H, with ROUGE/BERTScore as corroboration, which helps), some HotpotQA results show high variance (e.g., ASR 15.23 ± 1.56 for LLaMA3), and there is no statistical significance testing; also no results on larger models beyond ~8B, leaving the scalability of the defense unclear.

The theoretical contribution is loose: the reference model conditions in the proof (Eqs. 20-21, including the typo) and the Jensen's inequality bounding are somewhat ad hoc, and the Lemma only establishes asymptotic consistency rather than a tight guarantee; the connection motivates but does not justify the design rigorously.

Mechanistic claims (e.g., middle-layer concentration, key neurons in LLaMA reflecting 'instruction perception') are descriptive observations without deeper causal validation, though they are interesting and consistent with prior findings.

strengths: The core idea is interesting and somewhat novel: using neural (gradient-times-activation) attribution over the context KV cache to identify 'task-triggering' neurons, then masking them to defend against indirect prompt injection, without modifying prompts or adding test-time LLM calls.

The evaluation is relatively thorough for this line of work: three models, three datasets (SQuAD, HotpotQA, WildChat), comparisons with several prompt-engineering baselines, ablations on k, alpha, N, and pruning percentage p, plus transferability across attack types and an adaptive GCG-based attack study (Appendix G).

The paper attempts theoretical grounding by connecting the preferential attribution loss to an upper bound of the DPO objective (Theorem 1, Lemma 1), and reports additional free-form metrics (ROUGE, BERTScore) to support the response-quality claims.
The defense is positioned as complementary to existing detection/filtering and training-based approaches and is compatible with context caching, which is a practically relevant property.
weaknesses: Writing quality is significantly below ACL standards: pervasive grammatical errors, misspellings, and inconsistent terminology throughout ('perference', 'trigerring', 'Daramarking', 'differen values', 'interprete', 'we enforcing', 'SQUaD', 'With (20) and (20)', incomplete sentences such as 'resulting in the model understanding the context'). Many sentences require reconstruction, and Table 1/Figure 1 contain apparent errors (e.g., 'PICC' vs. 'IPCC'). This severely impedes clarity and suggests the manuscript was not carefully prepared.

The central empirical setup raises concerns about what is actually being learned: the pruning mask is computed from only N=8 samples drawn from a 400-prompt pool of the same dataset and then applied to all test prompts. It is unclear whether the result reflects a general 'data vs. instruction' mechanism or dataset/attack-distribution-specific artifacts. The transferability experiments (Tables 2, 5, Figure 5) partially address this but are limited in scope.

The claimed mechanistic interpretation ('pruning enforces the LLM to treat context purely as data') is asserted but not convincingly isolated from simpler explanations (e.g., generic corruption of context representations degrading instruction-following on the context span). The finding that pruning does not necessarily decrease F1(clean) is acknowledged but left under-analyzed.

The theoretical analysis has issues: the proof of Theorem 1 contains errors (Eq. 21 appears to be a typo for a wrong inequality, 'With (20) and (20)'), the direction/sign of the DPO upper bound is not carefully justified, and Lemma 1's 'association' is only asymptotic limits, which provides weak support for the practical loss in Eq. (13) with k=1.

The evaluation setup is small-scale and non-standard: very low absolute F1 scores (~25-29 on SQuAD/HotpotQA) differ substantially from typical QA performance, attributed to free-form generation, but the magnitude weakens confidence in the utility-preserving claims; the WildChat setup requires manually inserting an attack instruction, and ASR is judged via LLM-as-judge with GPT-4, which introduces additional noise not quantified.

The claim that CachePrune is 'immune' to the adaptive attack is overstated: the adaptive attack is trained on only 24 samples with modest budget, and the near-100% ASR on baselines vs. ~1-2% on CachePrune could reflect optimization difficulty rather than robustness; the authors' own explanation ('smoother embedding landscape') is speculative.

The method requires pre-known context boundaries, which the paper acknowledges but does not empirically evaluate under boundary uncertainty or realistic API templates, limiting practical applicability claims.

No code or artifact release is mentioned, which, combined with the many ambiguous implementation details (e.g., exact positive/negative sampling, thresholding procedure in Eq. 5), hampers reproducibility.

Baseline coverage is incomplete by design: fine-tuning-based and workflow-based defenses are excluded with a cost argument, but a small-scale comparison (even a subset) would substantially strengthen the contribution's positioning.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated defense: pruning task-triggering neurons in the context KV cache is a fresh angle on indirect prompt injection defense that leaves the prompt unchanged, requires no extra test-time LLM calls, and is compatible with context caching — a practical advantage over prompt-engineering and workflow-based baselines.

Sound methodological construction: the preferential attribution loss is carefully connected to a DPO upper bound (Theorem 1, Lemma 1), and design choices (most-probable-response sampling, trigger-token truncation, subset Φ for quality preservation, selective thresholding) are each motivated rather than ad hoc.
Sample efficiency is convincingly demonstrated: effective attribution with N=8 samples is a meaningful practical contribution versus fine-tuning-based defenses requiring hundreds of samples.

Comprehensive empirical validation: three models (LLaMA3-8B, Mistral-7B, Phi-3.5-mini), three datasets (SQuAD, HotpotQA, WildChat), ablations over k, α, p, Φ, and N, mask transferability across attack instructions and across code/text injection types, layer-distribution analysis, and an adaptive GCG attack in the appendix — the adaptive attack evaluation is particularly commendable and shows CachePrune retains low ASR where baselines collapse to ~100% ASR.
Additional free-form metrics (ROUGE, BERTScore) and released evaluation code snippets improve the credibility of the quality-preservation claims.

Compatible with prior work and transparently scoped: the authors clearly state assumptions (known context boundary, fixed templates) and position the method as complementary rather than a replacement.
weaknesses: Threat model assumptions limit generality: the pruning mask is learned from a handful of prompts with constructed poisoned/clean response pairs, requiring knowledge of the context boundary and an approximation of the most probable poisoned response (constructed via an auxiliary 'Answer this at the end' prompt). Robustness of the learned mask to substantially different or unseen attack distributions is tested only within a narrow family of attack instructions.

The theoretical portion is somewhat loose: Theorem 1's proof relies on an assumed reference model satisfying inequalities (20)-(21) with a typo in cross-reference, and Lemma 1's asymptotic arguments (e.g., bounding N_x^c by limited context length) are heuristic; the theory motivates but does not rigorously guarantee the empirical objective.

Some empirical claims could be better explained: the near-immunity of CachePrune to the adaptive GCG attack on LLaMA3-8B (7.71 vs ~100 ASR for baselines) is attributed to a 'smoother embedding landscape' without direct evidence; the claim that pruning may even improve F1 (clean) via 'informing the LLM of prompt structure' is speculative.

Reproducibility concerns: no explicit statement of code release; several hyperparameters (pool of 400 prompts, 3 trials, sampling procedure details) are described but the construction of poisoned responses involves manual/LLM-based steps that would be hard to replicate exactly.

Writing quality needs polish: numerous typos and grammatical errors throughout (e.g., 'trigerring', 'enforce the LLM interprete', 'ans metrics', 'perference', 'adaptuve'), and Figure 5's matrix-notation description is convoluted; these do not undermine the science but detract from presentation standards.

Comparisons exclude fine-tuning-based and test-time-workflow defenses (StruQ, SEP, FATH, TaskShield) on cost grounds; while defensible, a direct quality/robustness comparison even on a subset would strengthen the case that CachePrune is competitive rather than merely cheaper.
